title: Reverse Integer

understand.question: Given a signed 32-bit integer, how do we flip its digits backwards while keeping its minus sign and returning 0 if the flipped value overflows 32 bits?
understand.plainExplanation: Peel the last digit off x using remainder (% 10) and push it onto the back of rev by multiplying rev by 10 and adding that digit. Before multiplying by 10, check whether rev is about to exceed the 32-bit signed integer limits [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].
understand.outputMeaning: The digit-reversed integer, or 0 if reversing x falls outside [-2,147,483,648, 2,147,483,647].
rules: Trailing zeros disappear when reversed (for example, 420 reverses to 24).
Negative numbers stay negative (-420 reverses to -24).
If the reversed integer cannot fit in signed 32 bits [-2147483648, 2147483647], return 0.

terms.definition: Integers from INT_MIN (-2,147,483,648) up to INT_MAX (2,147,483,647).
Integer division toward zero (so -12 / 10 = -1 and -12 % 10 = -2 in C/Java/JS, whereas Python's // floors toward -infinity).

example1.whyValid: Popping digits from right to left yields 0, then 2, then 4 while preserving the negative sign, producing -24.

example2.whyEdgeCase: Reversing 1,534,236,469 gives 9,646,324,351, which exceeds INT_MAX (2,147,483,647), so we must detect overflow BEFORE multiplying rev * 10 and return 0.

dryRun.algorithmName: Digit Pop & Push with Pre-Overflow Guard

steps.title: Pop last digit 0 from -420
steps.description: Pop = -420 % 10 = 0, remaining x = -42. Since rev = 0 is safely inside [-214748364, 214748364], rev = 0 * 10 + 0 = 0.

steps.title: Pop 2 -> rev = -2
steps.description: Pop = -42 % 10 = -2 (or +2 with sign separated), remaining x = -4. Pre-overflow guard passes; rev becomes -2.

steps.title: Pop 4 -> guard safe -> return -24
steps.description: Pop = -4, remaining x = 0. Check -2 >= -214748364 (safe!), so rev = -2 * 10 + (-4) = -24. Loop ends because x == 0; return -24.

approaches.name: Math Pop & Push with 32-bit Overflow Guard
approaches.recommendedTradeOff: Uses pure integer arithmetic in O(log10 |x|) time and O(1) space, strictly staying within 32-bit integer arithmetic without allocating strings or 64-bit types.
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Repeatedly pop x % 10 and check rev against INT_MAX / 10 before rev * 10 + digit.
approaches.coreIdea: Pop digits one by one with % 10 and / 10. Before updating rev = rev * 10 + pop, verify that rev will not overflow [INT_MIN, INT_MAX].
steps: While x != 0: pop = remainder toward zero, x = truncated quotient x / 10.
If rev > INT_MAX / 10 or (rev == INT_MAX / 10 and pop > 7), return 0.
If rev < INT_MIN / 10 or (rev == INT_MIN / 10 and pop < -8), return 0.
Set rev = rev * 10 + pop and continue; return rev.
approaches.whyItWorks: Because INT_MAX = 2147483647 ends in 7 and INT_MIN = -2147483648 ends in -8, comparing rev against +/-214748364 catches every overflow one step before multiplication overflows.
approaches.whenToUse: Default optimal solution, especially in strict 32-bit environments.

complexity.variables: x = input integer (at most 10 digits for 32-bit)

approaches.name: String Reversal with Bounds Check
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Convert |x| to a string, reverse its characters, parse back, and clamp to 32-bit bounds.
approaches.coreIdea: Handle the sign separately, reverse the decimal digit string, parse it safely (using 64-bit / float / big-int), and return 0 if out of [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].
steps: Convert |x| to string, reverse characters, and parse integer val = sign * int(reversedStr).
If val < -2^31 or val > 2^31 - 1, return 0; else return val.
approaches.whyItWorks: String reversal handles trailing zeros automatically when parsed back to an integer.
approaches.whenToUse: Quick to write in languages with arbitrary-precision ints, though slower and uses extra string memory.
approaches.diagramNote: Separates '-', reverses digit characters ['4','2','0'] -> "024", parses 24, and reapplies sign.
